sourceCitations: [14] Department of National Defence, “Defence Energy and Environment Strategy—2023 Progress Update,” Ottawa, ON, Canada, 2024. Available: https://www.canada.ca/en/department-national-defence/corporate/reports-publications/defence-energy-environment-progress-2023.html
evidence.methodNotes: High-security depot operations including conditioned storage, ventilation, and standby generation.

activities.name: Military aviation (pkm)
activities.description: Representative fuel use for crewed military aviation missions allocated per person-kilometre equivalent.

sourceCitations: [40] NATO Science & Technology Organization, “Operational Energy Metrics for NATO Missions,” Brussels, Belgium, 2023. Available: https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/topics_197175.htm
evidence.methodNotes: Midpoint of NATO operational energy intensity range for tactical airlift and fighter missions.

activities.name: Munitions detonated
activities.description: Detonating one metric tonne of mixed munitions during exercises or combat operations.

sourceCitations: [3] Conflict and Environment Observatory, “Explosive Materials Supply Chain Emissions,” 2023. Available: https://ceobs.org/report-explosive-materials-supply-chain-emissions/
evidence.methodNotes: Munitions detonation: 0.42 tCO2e/t TNT-equivalent from explosive oxidation (0.30 t), casing vaporization (0.08 t), and propellant residue combustion (0.04 t); bounds 0.30–0.55 tCO2e/t for composition variation.

activities.name: Munitions detonation event
activities.description: Modeled emissions from a coordinated munitions detonation scenario.

sourceCitations: [3] Conflict and Environment Observatory, “Explosive Materials Supply Chain Emissions,” 2023. Available: https://ceobs.org/report-explosive-materials-supply-chain-emissions/
evidence.methodNotes: Coordinated munitions detonation event: 30 t TNT-equivalent baseline (12.5 tCO2e) representing mixed artillery/rocket strike package; bounds 5–25 tCO2e/event for engagement scale 10–60 t TNT.

activities.name: Ammunition production (t)
activities.description: Cradle-to-gate emissions for producing one tonne of mixed-calibre munitions.

evidence.methodNotes: Synthesised from SIPRI/CEOBS embodied emissions factors for ammunition plants.

activities.name: Military naval shipping (tonne-km)
activities.description: Marine fuel intensity for naval logistics and combat vessels allocated per tonne-kilometre moved.

evidence.methodNotes: Averages NATO auxiliary and propulsion fuel burn per tonne-kilometre for naval logistics.

activities.name: Armoured vehicle production (unit)
activities.description: Embodied emissions for producing a main battle tank or heavy infantry fighting vehicle.

evidence.methodNotes: Embodied emissions midpoint for main battle tank manufacture with composite armour packages.

activities.name: Military ground vehicles (km)
activities.description: Armoured and tactical ground vehicle fuel burn per kilometre travelled.

evidence.methodNotes: Representative JP-8 consumption for mixed armoured ground fleets under combined arms training tempo.

activities.name: Wildfire incident
activities.description: Modeled wildfire incident covering suppression logistics and mutual aid response.

sourceCitations: [15] Environment and Climate Change Canada, “National Inventory Report 1990–2023: Greenhouse Gas Sources and Sinks in Canada,” Ottawa, ON, Canada, 2025. Available: https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2025/eccc/En81-4-2025-1-eng.pdf
evidence.methodNotes: Large wildfire incident (5,000 ha baseline): suppression operations add ~170 tCO2e (aerial sorties 120 t, ground fleet 35 t, camp logistics 15 t) atop burn emissions; bounds 450–1,250 tCO2e/event reflect fire size 2k–10k ha.

activities.name: Wildfire burned area
activities.description: Burning one hectare of forested land in a wildfire.

sourceCitations: [15] Environment and Climate Change Canada, “National Inventory Report 1990–2023: Greenhouse Gas Sources and Sinks in Canada,” Ottawa, ON, Canada, 2025. Available: https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2025/eccc/En81-4-2025-1-eng.pdf
evidence.methodNotes: Boreal forest wildfire: 45 tCO2e/ha burned integrating crown fire (30 t/ha), surface fuel (12 t/ha), and soil carbon release (3 t/ha); bounds 25–65 tCO2e/ha span temperate mixed to boreal black spruce stands.

activities.name: Mixed MSW sent to energy-from-waste
activities.description: Municipal mixed solid waste combusted in a waste-to-energy facility.

sourceCitations: [19] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, “Waste Reduction Model (WARM), Version 15,” Oct. 2023. Available: https://www.epa.gov/warm/versions-waste-reduction-model-warm#15
evidence.methodNotes: EPA WARM v15 mixed MSW combustion for energy recovery reports ~0.267 MTCO2e per short ton; converted to 295 gCO2e/kg assuming 907.185 kg per short ton and retaining ±35% bounds for facility energy offsets.

activities.name: Mixed MSW managed via landfill
activities.description: Municipal mixed solid waste routed to a landfill with landfill-gas recovery.

sourceCitations: [19] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, “Waste Reduction Model (WARM), Version 15,” Oct. 2023. Available: https://www.epa.gov/warm/versions-waste-reduction-model-warm#15
evidence.methodNotes: EPA WARM v15 mixed MSW landfilling (national average LFG recovery, typical collection) gives 0.438 MTCO2e per short ton disposed; converted to 482.8 gCO2e/kg using 907.185 kg per short ton.

activities.name: Potable water treatment & delivery
activities.description: Treated drinking water pumped through Toronto’s distribution network.

sourceCitations: [57] Toronto Water, “2023 Drinking Water System Annual Report,” City of Toronto, Feb. 2024. Available: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/water-environment/tap-water-in-toronto/drinking-water-quality-reports/
evidence.methodNotes: Toronto Water 2023 annual report cites ≈72 kt CO2e scope 1+2 emissions over ~0.40 billion m³ supplied; intensity rounded to 0.18 kgCO2e/m³ with ±30% bounds for year-to-year energy mix swings.

activities.name: Music streaming—standard quality per hour
activities.description: One hour of standard-quality audio streaming.

activities.name: Surface-ocean pH decline (ΔpH/decade)

evidence.methodNotes: Pan-Arctic thaw emissions aggregated as Pg CO₂e per year.

activities.name: Refrigerator operation (year)
activities.description: Annual household refrigerator or freezer electricity use and average refrigerant leakage.

evidence.methodNotes: Assumes 600 kWh/year refrigerator electricity on the Ontario grid (16.8 kgCO2e) with 10% leakage of a 0.6 kg HFC-134a charge (≈128 kgCO2e) per IEA 2024 cooling efficiency guidance and AR6 GWP.

activities.name: Refrigerator unit produced
activities.description: Embodied emissions for manufacturing a household refrigerator or freezer including initial refrigerant charge.

activities.name: Supermarket cold storage (kg food-year)
activities.description: Electricity and refrigerant leakage intensity per kilogram of food kept in supermarket cold storage for one year.

sourceCitations: [20] Food and Agriculture Organization and International Energy Agency, “Cold Chain Energy and Emission Factors,” 2024. Available: https://www.fao.org/energy/newsroom/detail/en/c/1654324/
evidence.methodNotes: FAO/IEA 2024 supermarket cold-chain study: 12 kWh/kg-food-year Ontario electricity (≈336 gCO2e) plus 8% annual leakage of 0.02 kg R448A per kg throughput (~164 gCO2e).

activities.name: Air-conditioner operation (year)
activities.description: Annual electricity demand and refrigerant leakage for a residential or light-commercial air-conditioning system.

sourceCitations: [28] International Energy Agency Cool Coalition, “Cooling for All: Operational Benchmarks,” 2024. Available: https://www.coolcoalition.org/resources/
evidence.methodNotes: Combines 1,200 kWh/year AC electricity on Ontario grid (≈33.6 kgCO2e) with 6% annual leakage of a 1.5 kg R410A charge (~366 kgCO2e) from IEA Cool Coalition 2024 operational benchmarks.

activities.name: Air-conditioner unit produced
activities.description: Embodied emissions for manufacturing a split or central air-conditioning system including initial refrigerant charge.

sourceCitations: [60] Technology and Economic Assessment Panel, “TEAP 2023 Assessment Report—HFC Phase-down,” United Nations Environment Programme, 2023. Available: https://ozone.unep.org/assessment-panels/teap
evidence.methodNotes: UNEP TEAP 2023 split/central AC embodied intensity including compressor, coil, and cabinet manufacturing plus 1.5 kg R410A initial fill at AR6 GWP.

activities.name: River/ocean hypoxia (km²·yr)

evidence.methodNotes: Aggregate proxy for N₂O/CH₄ feedback and lost sink services per km²-year.

activities.name: Facebook usage

sourceCitations: [23] R. Hintemann and S. Hinterholzer, “Energy Consumption of Digital Services: Streaming vs. Social Media,” Borderstep Institute and IITP, 2022. Available: https://www.iitp.de/digital-carbon-footprint
evidence.methodNotes: Hintemann & Hinterholzer Facebook estimate (0.06 kgCO2e/hr) tuned with SRC.META.SR.2023 operational efficiency disclosures and SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 network/data-centre intensity ranges.

activities.name: Instagram usage
activities.description: Scrolling and watching media on Instagram for 1 hour.

sourceCitations: [23] R. Hintemann and S. Hinterholzer, “Energy Consumption of Digital Services: Streaming vs. Social Media,” Borderstep Institute and IITP, 2022. Available: https://www.iitp.de/digital-carbon-footprint
evidence.methodNotes: Instagram hour derived from SRC.HINTEMANN2022 mobile-focused scenario with 70% smartphone, 20% tablet, 10% desktop device mix anchored to SRC.META.SR.2023 efficiency improvements and SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 bandwidth intensity; ±40% bounds (50–150 gCO2e/hr) follow SRC.MALMODIN.2018.

activities.name: LinkedIn usage
activities.description: Browsing LinkedIn for 1 hour.

sourceCitations: [23] R. Hintemann and S. Hinterholzer, “Energy Consumption of Digital Services: Streaming vs. Social Media,” Borderstep Institute and IITP, 2022. Available: https://www.iitp.de/digital-carbon-footprint
evidence.methodNotes: LinkedIn browsing intensity (0.05 kgCO2e/hr) via SRC.HINTEMANN2022 knowledge-worker profile, cross-checked with SRC.MALMODIN.2018 ICT footprint ratios and SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 network data.

activities.name: Snapchat usage

sourceCitations: [23] R. Hintemann and S. Hinterholzer, “Energy Consumption of Digital Services: Streaming vs. Social Media,” Borderstep Institute and IITP, 2022. Available: https://www.iitp.de/digital-carbon-footprint
evidence.methodNotes: Snapchat hour from SRC.HINTEMANN2022 handset-intensive scenario, adjusted with SRC.META.SR.2023 infrastructure efficiency and SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 bandwidth ranges; ±40% uncertainty from SRC.MALMODIN.2018.

activities.name: TikTok usage
activities.description: Watching short-form video on TikTok for 1 hour.

sourceCitations: [23] R. Hintemann and S. Hinterholzer, “Energy Consumption of Digital Services: Streaming vs. Social Media,” Borderstep Institute and IITP, 2022. Available: https://www.iitp.de/digital-carbon-footprint
evidence.methodNotes: TikTok per-hour footprint (0.15 kgCO2e/hr) from SRC.HINTEMANN2022 short-video profile using 85% smartphone, 10% tablet, 5% desktop usage mix with network intensity anchored to SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 and expanded bounds (80–250 gCO2e/hr) reflecting SRC.MALMODIN.2018 variability.

activities.name: Twitter/X usage

evidence.methodNotes: Twitter/X browsing electricity (0.055 kgCO2e/hr) per SRC.HINTEMANN2022, validated against SRC.IEA.DIGITAL.NETWORKS.2023 network/device ranges and broader ICT intensity bounds from SRC.MALMODIN.2018.

activities.name: YouTube usage
